Humans can live for 3 weeks without food, 3 days without water... but only about 3 minutes without air to breathe. Think about that. Comparatively speaking, breathable air is the most vital to life of any substance we require. The question for future Mars inhabitants then is, how can we best conserve the air that is available.

Should there be air tanks strategically placed throughout the entire habitable structure? Yes of course. One never knows when a failure of either walls, windows or airlock seals might occur so it would be a very wise policy to ensure readily available oxygen tanks stored in each and every section of the habitat. And each section should be able to be sealed off from adjoining sections, just in case of catastrophic failure or meteor strike. When you depend on something for survival it's quite a good idea to have an extra supply (lots of extra supply) of that thing readily available and always on hand.

But disaster won't strike every day. In fact, if a Mars habitat is constructed far enough underground there would be far less chance that any outside event would cause problems for those within the habitat itself. But the maxim better safe than sorry definitely absolutely and positively will apply to any and all human habitations on Mars. To do otherwise would be quite foolish.

What about the rest of the time, when all is well and things all go to plan. Humans living and working on Mars would need to recycle the air so that a given volume of air could be used indefinitely. And as anyone who has flown on an airplane knows, recycled air is shared air so any airborne bacteria, fungus or virus would swiftly spread throughout. A single person with a contagion could, theoretically, wipe out an entire Mars city if care is not taken, if proper technological precautions are not taken. So, how does one remove all those nasty little organisms so small that one can't even see them?

Air filtration is a viable option but the filters would need to be replaced eventually, and since it's likely that these supplies would come from Earth (at least initially until manufacturing facilities on Mars using locally available materials are built). Thus, any item that is "disposable" is both an unnecessary cost and a danger to all who would rely on it.

So any airborne pathogens would need to be removed or inactivated before any further processing of the air could be done. In many places like hospital "isolation rooms" where immunocompromised patients are the air needs to be filtered as well to ensure the life of the patient. The same would apply for everyone on Mars. Then the CO2 can be removed (by plants or by other means). But if pathogens aren't removed first there is a chance that the personnel working in whatever would be the equivalent of Mars farms would be exposed and the contagion would spread via multiple vectors (the farmers themselves). So it is critical that the first step in the air recycling process must be to remove any such biological agents.

Some of you might find it particularly unusual that I am exposed to ads, and actually, I am not on my computer. On my phone I am ignorant and primitive and haven't taken steps to block and avoid advertisements due to the low quality of my phone. As a result of this, I've realized the ignorance and primitiveness of such advertising.

The most common and effective forms of advertisements before the internet gained popularity would probably be the TV commercial. The Super Bowl even was famous for it's funny, outrageous, and memorable commercials back then. They're trying to keep this alive, but a lot of gimmicks and stuff aren't that special and interesting anymore. Of course on the other hand there is still radio, and with it there is radio advertisement, which may come in second place for it's prevalence and effectiveness. Print advertising is still going, but as magazines and newspapers become a thing of the past so will print advertising.

Since video sites are supposed to host videos, the philosophy for video site advertising is to take TV commercials and put them on the internet. It doesn't seem to be acknowledged that sometimes people use video sites as a sort of radio that they listen to while not looking at the device. So what happens is some companies foolishly make TV-style ads that depend on visuals for people that are using the platform as a glorified radio. The fact that people won't even know what you're advertising since they're not looking hasn't occurred to some of these ad makers. The question of whether the user is using it like a TV or a radio is repudiated. Of course video platforms could take steps to try to identify whether a "video" is more of an audio file the person has playing while not looking. For such instances the advertising should intelligently be switched to radio-style to use audio to promote the product.

Another issue I've noticed is sound differential problems. I listen to a lot of talk videos in a no-looking radio-style, and often times the commentators do not have professional sound equipment or adjustments. This results in low volume levels that require you to turn the volume up. When an ad comes in with no acknowledgement of this, often times it is too damn loud. The resulting reaction from me is, "What is this obnoxiously loud garbage?" Of course this is not a state an advertiser would want someone to be in while being exposed to their ad. Of course this problem could easily be solved by volume analysis of a video with a sound adjusted ad to follow. Yes, advertisers generally go for a little louder than the typical TV or radio content but making sure it is a little and not a lot is the key to success. Obviously, the opposite situation of an advertisement too quiet to be heard would also be a problem, but generally, they're all too damn loud.

Aside from this it seems the short, five-second ad is the gold standard for video site advertising. People aren't as comfortable with ads on the internet as they are on TV due to the high level of user control. With TV or radio style adjustments and sound level acknowledgements, they would be even more effective.
